turns.text: What is a square root, actually?

turn.asked: What is a square root, actually?
turn.reply: Great question! A square root is the opposite of squaring a number. If you square a number (multiply it by itself), the square root undoes that. For example, 3 × 3 = 9, so the square root of 9 is 3. √2 is the number that, when multiplied by itself, gives exactly 2. turns.ask: Why do we multiply the remainder by 10 each time?

testCase.good: Each step moves to the next decimal place (tenths, hundredths), which is the same as bringing down a 0. Concrete with this board's remainder.

turns.text: Why do we multiply the remainder by 10 each time?

turn.asked: Why do we multiply the remainder by 10 each time?
turn.reply:
Great question! Think of it this way: when you have a remainder of 3 after dividing 3 by 8, you can't divide 3 by 8 directly because 3 is smaller. So you're asking "how many tenths do I have?" — and 3 ones is the same as 30 tenths (3 × 10). Then you divide 30 by 8 to get 3 tenths (that's the 3 you already see after the decimal point), with 6 tenths left over. Next, those 6 tenths become 60 hundredths (6 × 10), and so on. Each time, you're moving to the next smaller decimal place — tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and each place is 10 times smaller, so you multiply by 10 to convert.

Now, go ahead and tap the division to work out the next digit! The board is waiting for you. 😊

turn.reply:
Great question! Here's the key idea: a decimal ends (terminates) when the denominator, in simplest form, only has the prime factors 2 and/or 5. That's because our number system is base 10, and 10 = 2 × 5.

1 ÷ 8: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, so only 2s — that's why 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125, nice and finished.

1 ÷ 3: 3 has a prime factor 3, which isn't 2 or 5, so the decimal keeps going: 0.333...

Now, look at the three options on the board. Which denominators have only 2s and 5s as prime factors? Try figuring that out and pick the one you think ends!
